title: Ring
body:
A set with **two** operations, $+$ and $\times$, that interact the way they do in $\mathbb{Z}$.
A [[Group]] has one operation; a ring is the next structure up, and the model to keep in mind is
always the integers.

$(R, +, \times)$ is a ring when:

| Under $+$ | Under $\times$ | Together |
|---|---|---|
| abelian group: closed, associative, commutative, zero, negatives | closed and associative | distributive: $a(b+c) = ab+ac$ and $(a+b)c = ac+bc$ |

Distributivity is the only axiom that mentions both operations, and it is therefore the only
thing making a ring more than two unrelated structures on one set.

What is deliberately **not** required: multiplicative commutativity, a multiplicative identity,
and multiplicative inverses. Different textbooks assume different subsets of those; this course
uses "ring with 1" for the standard examples and says so when it matters.

## The ladder

Each rung adds one requirement, and the whole of blocks 3 and 4 is climbing it:

```
ring                  +, ×, distributive
 └ commutative ring   ab = ba
    └ integral domain  has 1 ≠ 0, and no zero divisors
       └ field         every non-zero element has an inverse
```

| Example | Commutative | Domain | Field |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| $\mathbb{Z}$ | yes | yes | **no** (2 has no inverse) |
| $\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}$ | yes | yes | yes |
| $\mathbb{Z}_6$ | yes | **no** ($2 \cdot 3 = 0$) | no |
| $\mathbb{Z}_p$, $p$ prime | yes | yes | yes; see [[Finite Field]] |
| $n \times n$ matrices | **no** | no | no |
| $F[x]$, polynomials over a field | yes | yes | no; see [[Polynomial Ring]] |

$\mathbb{Z}$ is the integral domain that is not a field, and that gap is the reason the course
exists: it is where divisibility, primes, and factorisation live. In a field everything divides
everything and there is nothing left to say.

## Zero divisors, the thing that goes wrong

A **zero divisor** is a non-zero $a$ with $ab = 0$ for some non-zero $b$. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$,
$2 \cdot 3 = 0$. Their presence is exactly the failure of cancellation: $ab = ac$ no longer
gives $b = c$, so ordinary algebra breaks. An **integral domain** is a commutative ring with 1
and no zero divisors, which is the minimum needed for the manipulations you have been doing
since school to remain valid.

By the same argument as in [[Modular Arithmetic]]: $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a domain exactly when $n$ is
prime, and for finite rings domain and field turn out to be the same condition.

## Ideals, and why quotients look like $\mathbb{Z}_n$

An **ideal** $I \le R$ is an additive subgroup that absorbs multiplication: $ra \in I$ for every
$r \in R$, $a \in I$. It is the ring-theoretic analogue of a normal subgroup, and it is what you
quotient by. $R/I$ has the [[Coset|cosets]] of $I$ as elements.

The example is not new: $n\mathbb{Z}$ is an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$, and

$$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}_n$$

so modular arithmetic *is* a quotient ring, and the congruence classes are cosets. Every ideal of
$\mathbb{Z}$ has the form $n\mathbb{Z}$, generated by a single element, which is the structural
restatement of Bézout in [[Euclidean Algorithm]]: the ideal generated by $a$ and $b$ is generated
by $\gcd(a,b)$ alone.

Kernels of ring [[Homomorphism|homomorphisms]] are exactly the ideals, mirroring groups.

## Where the vault already uses rings

- **$\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$** is the ring an $n$-bit register implements. See
  [[Integer Representation]] and [[Modular Arithmetic]].
- **Polynomials over $\mathbb{Z}_2$** are the objects behind cyclic redundancy checks and
  [[Error Correcting Code|error correcting codes]], with $GF(2^8)$ the workhorse; see
  [[Finite Field]].
- **Matrices** are the standard non-commutative ring, which is why $AB \ne BA$ in
  [[Matrix Multiplication]] is a fact about the structure rather than an annoyance.
